topic: a city council's decision to replace a public park with affordable housing
wrong_topic: a review of a new restaurant opening downtown
text: Last Tuesday the council voted six to three to rezone Linden Park. The fourteen-acre green space, home to a community garden and two aging baseball diamonds, will give way to roughly four hundred apartments, at least half of them priced below market rate. Supporters packed the chamber with signs reading "Homes, Not Hedges." They pointed out that the median rent in the city has risen forty percent in five years and that the waiting list for subsidized units now exceeds eleven thousand households. Opponents, many of them longtime residents of the surrounding blocks, argued that the park is the only open space within walking distance for thousands of children, and that the council ignored two vacant parking lots owned by the city just a mile away. The mayor, who had promised during her campaign to protect green space, abstained. A spokesperson for the developer said construction could begin within eighteen months, pending an environmental review. Several residents have already announced plans to file a lawsuit, claiming that the public notice for the hearing was posted only on the city website and never mailed to nearby households. The council member who introduced the measure called the lawsuit a delaying tactic and said that every month of delay means more families leaving the city. Whether the decision represents courage or betrayal seems to depend largely on which side of the park fence one lives on.

topic: a company's new policy of monitoring remote employees' keystrokes
wrong_topic: a scientific study about sleep and memory
text: Starting next month, every remote employee at Brightline Logistics will install software that records keystrokes, active application time, and a screenshot every ten minutes. The company's chief operating officer described the change in an internal memo as a step toward "fairness and transparency," noting that some teams had complained about colleagues who appeared to be online but delivered little. The memo promised that the data would be used only in aggregate and never for individual discipline without a manager's review. Employees reacted quickly. Within hours, an anonymous survey circulated on a workplace forum, and more than seventy percent of respondents said they would consider leaving. Some argued that productivity should be judged by results, not by mouse movements. Others quietly admitted that they had seen coworkers exploit the flexibility of remote work and were not entirely opposed. A labor lawyer consulted by a local newspaper said the policy is legal in most states as long as employees are informed in writing. The company's quarterly earnings, released the same week, showed a modest decline in margins, which some employees believe is the real motivation. Management has not responded to requests for comment on that point. For now, the software rollout remains on schedule, and the memo ends with a line that has been quoted widely: "Trust is built when everyone can see the same picture."

topic: a student athlete being disqualified after a positive test for a cold medicine
wrong_topic: the history of medieval trade routes
text: Mara Okafor had trained for four years for the regional championship. She won the 800 meters by nearly two seconds, the fastest time in the state this season. Three days later, the athletic association announced that her result had been voided. A routine test had detected a stimulant found in a common over-the-counter cold medicine, which she says she took the night before the race because of a sore throat. Her coach insists that no one ever told the team that the medicine was on the banned list, and that the list itself is a forty-page document written in technical language. The association responded that every athlete signs a form acknowledging responsibility for anything they ingest, and that the rule exists precisely because intent is impossible to prove. The runner-up, who now holds the title, said in a brief statement that she felt sorry for Okafor but believed the rules must apply to everyone equally. A petition asking for the decision to be reversed has collected over twenty thousand signatures. Some former athletes have signed it; others have publicly warned that making exceptions would open the door to abuse. Okafor's scholarship offer from a university is now under review. She has not raced since, and her family says she rarely leaves the house.

topic: a town debating whether to remove a statue of its founder
wrong_topic: instructions for assembling furniture
text: The bronze statue of Elias Harrow has stood in front of the town library since 1911. Harrow founded the town, donated the land for its first school, and paid for the library itself. He also, according to records uncovered last year by a graduate student, made much of his fortune by evicting tenant farmers during a drought and buying their land at a fraction of its value. Since the records were published, the statue has been splashed with red paint twice. At a crowded public meeting, a retired teacher said that removing the statue would erase the town's history and that every historical figure had flaws. A young organizer replied that a statue is not history but honor, and that history would remain in the books and the archive. Several speakers proposed a compromise: keep the statue but add a plaque describing the evictions. Others objected that a plaque would be easy to ignore. The library board, which technically owns the statue, has said it will follow the result of a nonbinding vote scheduled for the spring. Descendants of both Harrow and the evicted families still live in town, and some of them attend the same church. One of them told a reporter that she was tired of being asked which side she was on.

topic: a hospital rationing a scarce drug using a lottery
wrong_topic: a travel guide to coastal beaches
text: When the shortage began, the hospital had enough of the drug for roughly one in three eligible patients. The ethics committee met for two days. In the end, they chose a lottery: every patient who met the medical criteria would be entered, and a computer would select who received treatment each week. The committee chair explained that any other method, such as prioritizing younger patients or those with better prognoses, would require doctors to make judgments about whose life mattered more. Some families accepted the decision with resignation. Others were furious. A man whose mother was not selected said it felt like gambling with lives, and asked why the hospital had not prioritized the sickest patients first. A physician on the committee responded that the sickest patients were often the least likely to benefit, and that choosing them would mean fewer lives saved overall. A local politician demanded an investigation, while a national bioethics group praised the hospital for its transparency. Meanwhile, the manufacturer has said that new supply will not arrive for at least four months. Nurses report that the weekly announcement of results has become the hardest hour of their shift. The committee has agreed to revisit the policy monthly, but no one has proposed an alternative that the members find clearly fairer.

topic: a school district banning smartphones during the entire school day
wrong_topic: a recipe for homemade sourdough bread
text: Starting next month, students in the Riverside district will have to lock their phones in magnetic pouches from the first bell until dismissal. The school board approved the policy four to one after a survey found that teachers spent an average of eleven minutes per class asking students to put devices away. Principals at two pilot schools reported fewer fights in hallways and a small rise in library visits during lunch. Parents, however, are divided. Some said they were relieved that their children would finally talk to each other at lunch. Others pointed out that the district had three lockdown drills last year and asked how they were supposed to reach their children in an emergency. A group of students with diabetes who use phone apps to monitor their glucose levels will receive exemptions, but the process for requesting one has not been published. The pouches cost about thirty dollars each, and the district plans to pay for them with money originally set aside for new science equipment. The only board member who voted against the plan said the policy treats a symptom rather than the cause. A teacher at the high school said that students would simply find new ways to distract themselves, as they always have. The superintendent said the district would review attendance and grades at the end of the semester before deciding whether to keep the rule.

topic: a bakery owner refusing to hire applicants who have criminal records
wrong_topic: the migration patterns of arctic birds
text: When a popular downtown bakery posted a job listing that stated applicants with a criminal record need not apply, the reaction online was swift. Within two days the post had been shared thousands of times, and a local advocacy group organized a small protest outside the shop. The owner, who has run the bakery for nineteen years, said in an interview that she was robbed by a former employee five years ago and lost nearly twelve thousand dollars. She said she has a right to protect her business and the six people who work for her. The city passed a fair-chance hiring ordinance three years ago, but it applies only to employers with fifteen or more workers, so the bakery appears to be within the law. Supporters of the protest said that blanket exclusions make it nearly impossible for people leaving prison to rebuild their lives, and that most people with records were convicted of nonviolent offenses decades ago. Several regular customers said they would keep buying bread there because they trust the owner and like the staff. One of the current employees, who asked not to be named, said she had a conviction from twenty years ago that she never disclosed. A city council member has proposed lowering the threshold of the ordinance to five employees, and a hearing is scheduled for next month.

topic: a city installing facial recognition cameras in its subway stations
wrong_topic: a guide to growing tomatoes on a balcony
text: Commuters in the city's subway system will soon pass under more than two hundred new cameras equipped with facial recognition software. Transit officials say the system will be used only to find missing persons and suspects wanted for violent crimes, and that images of everyone else will be deleted within forty-eight hours. The contract, worth about nine million dollars, was approved without a public vote as part of a larger security budget. Officials pointed to a rise in assaults on train platforms last year and said the cameras helped identify a man who pushed a passenger onto the tracks during a trial run. Civil liberties groups argued that no independent body will audit how the data is used, and that similar systems in other cities misidentified people with darker skin at much higher rates. A spokesperson for the vendor said its latest model had an error rate below one percent in internal tests but declined to release the test data. Some riders interviewed at a busy station said they had nothing to hide and felt safer knowing the cameras were there. Others said they would start wearing masks again. The transit authority's own privacy officer resigned last week, saying only that she disagreed with the direction of the agency. The cameras are scheduled to go live in the spring.

topic: a pharmaceutical company raising the price of an old insulin product
wrong_topic: a beginner's guide to playing chess
text: A drug maker announced this week that it will raise the list price of one of its oldest insulin products by thirty-two percent, citing the cost of upgrading a manufacturing plant that regulators had cited for contamination risks. The insulin has been on the market for more than twenty years, and the patent expired long ago, but only two companies produce comparable versions. Patient groups said the decision will hurt people who are uninsured or whose plans have high deductibles, many of whom already ration their doses at the end of the month. The company responded that most insured patients pay a fixed copay that will not change, and that it offers a savings card that caps monthly costs for those who qualify. Critics noted that the savings card requires an application, proof of income, and renewal every six months. An economist who studies the drug industry said that the plant upgrade was real and expensive, but that the company's insulin division reported a profit margin above forty percent last year. Two senators have written to the company asking for a detailed breakdown of its costs. A nurse at a free clinic said she now spends part of every shift searching for donated vials. The new price takes effect on the first of next month.

topic: a university accepting a large donation from a fossil fuel company to fund climate research
wrong_topic: the rules of professional tennis
text: The state university confirmed on Friday that it has accepted a fifty million dollar gift from a major oil and gas company to establish a new center for climate and energy research. University leaders called the donation the largest in the school's history and said it will fund twenty new faculty positions and graduate fellowships over ten years. The agreement states that the company will have no control over research topics or publications, but it will hold one seat on the center's advisory board. A group of faculty members published an open letter saying that the arrangement creates an appearance of conflict and that researchers may avoid conclusions that would anger the donor. Students held a sit-in at the administration building, and the campus newspaper published an editorial calling the deal a public relations purchase. Other professors, including several climate scientists, said the field is chronically underfunded and that refusing the money would not reduce emissions by a single ton. The company's chief sustainability officer said it wants to support independent science on how to lower emissions from its own operations. The university's president said all research produced by the center will be published in full, regardless of its findings. The faculty senate plans to vote on a nonbinding resolution about the gift next week.

topic: a referee's controversial decision that decided a national football final
wrong_topic: how to care for a houseplant
text: In the ninety-third minute of the national cup final, with the score tied at one, the referee awarded a penalty after a defender's hand touched the ball inside the box. The video review lasted almost four minutes. Replays showed the ball striking the defender's arm from less than a meter away after deflecting off his own knee. The striker converted the penalty, and the match ended two to one. The losing team's coach said after the game that the rule was applied correctly but that the rule itself is absurd, because no player can move his arm out of the way in that time. The league's refereeing committee issued a statement saying that the defender's arm was extended away from his body and therefore made his silhouette larger, which the current law treats as an offense. Several former referees said on television that they would not have given the penalty, while others said the decision was textbook. Fans of the losing club gathered outside the federation headquarters the next morning, and the referee's family has reportedly received threats. The federation said it would ask the international rules body to clarify the handball law before next season. The winning team's captain said only that his side had created more chances over the full ninety minutes.

topic: a landlord evicting tenants to convert an apartment building into short-term vacation rentals
wrong_topic: a documentary about deep-sea creatures
text: Tenants of a forty-unit apartment building near the waterfront received notices last month telling them their leases would not be renewed. The new owner, an investment firm that bought the building in the spring, plans to renovate the units and rent them by the night to tourists. Most of the tenants have lived in the building for more than ten years, and several are elderly or disabled. Under state law, landlords may decline to renew leases with sixty days of notice, and the firm has offered each household a payment equal to two months of rent. A tenant organizer said that comparable apartments in the neighborhood now rent for nearly twice what residents currently pay, and that two months of rent will not cover a deposit and moving costs. A representative of the firm said the building had been poorly maintained by the previous owner and that the renovation will add jobs and tourist spending to the area. The city has a rule limiting short-term rentals in residential zones, but the building sits on a parcel that was rezoned for mixed use five years ago. Local restaurant owners are split, with some welcoming more visitors and others worried about losing regular customers. A city council member said she will introduce a bill to close the zoning gap, though it would not apply retroactively.

topic: a hospital using an artificial intelligence system to decide which patients get follow-up care
wrong_topic: the history of jazz music in New Orleans
text: A large hospital network has begun using a software model to flag which discharged patients should receive follow-up calls from nurses. The model scores each patient on the likelihood of being readmitted within thirty days, and only those above a threshold are called. Hospital administrators say the program reduced readmissions by nine percent in its first year and allowed a limited nursing staff to focus on the patients who need help most. An analysis by a group of outside researchers, however, found that the model relied heavily on past health spending as a signal of need. Because patients with less access to care tend to have lower spending, the researchers argued, the model may systematically underestimate how sick they are. The hospital said it has since removed spending as a direct input but declined to share the updated model for independent review, citing a contract with the vendor. Several nurses said privately that they sometimes call patients who fall just below the threshold because the score does not match what they saw on the ward. A patient advocate said that people should be told when software has influenced their care. The vendor said its product is a decision support tool and that clinicians always have the final word. State regulators have asked the hospital to submit data on outcomes by race and income.

topic: a town rejecting a proposed wind farm on its hills
wrong_topic: a review of a science fiction novel
text: After a meeting that ran past midnight, the planning board of a small hill town voted against a proposal to build twelve wind turbines on a ridge overlooking the valley. The developer had promised to pay the town about four hundred thousand dollars a year in taxes and lease fees, which would nearly double the town's road budget. Supporters, including several farmers who would have leased land for the turbines, said the project offered the town a rare source of income and a way to contribute to cleaner energy. Opponents argued that the turbines, each taller than a thirty-story building, would ruin views that draw summer visitors, and they raised concerns about noise and the effect on migrating birds. A study commissioned by the developer found that noise at the nearest home would stay below state limits, but residents questioned the study because the developer paid for it. The board chair said the decision came down to the town's own zoning rules, which limit structures on ridgelines to forty feet. The state energy office has said it is behind on its renewable targets and is considering a law that would let the state override local zoning for large clean energy projects. The developer said it would appeal the decision and look at other sites in the meantime.

topic: a newspaper publishing the leaked private messages of a political candidate
wrong_topic: tips for training a puppy
text: Three weeks before the election, a regional newspaper published excerpts from private messages sent by a candidate for governor to a former campaign aide. In the messages, the candidate made dismissive remarks about rural voters and joked about a rival's health. The newspaper said it received the messages from an anonymous source and verified them by comparing metadata and confirming details with two people who were part of the conversations. The candidate's campaign called the publication an invasion of privacy and suggested the messages had been obtained illegally, possibly by hacking the aide's account. The newspaper's editor said that the paper did not know how the source obtained the messages and that the public interest in the candidate's views outweighed privacy concerns. A journalism ethics professor said the case was difficult, because the remarks revealed something about the candidate's attitudes but were made in a context the candidate believed was private. Polls taken after the story show a small drop in the candidate's support, within the margin of error. The former aide said she did not leak the messages and has filed a police report about unauthorized access to her account. Other newspapers in the state have chosen not to republish the excerpts. The candidate apologized for the remarks about the rival's health but not for the comments about voters.

topic: a factory closing and moving its production overseas
wrong_topic: the life cycle of butterflies
text: The last shift at the appliance factory on the east side of town ended on Thursday afternoon. The company that owns the plant announced in the spring that it would move production to a facility abroad where labor costs are roughly one fifth of what it pays here. Six hundred and forty workers lost their jobs, many of whom had worked at the plant for more than two decades. The company said that it had lost money on its washing machine line for three consecutive years because of competition from cheaper imports, and that keeping the plant open would have put the entire business at risk. Union leaders said the company had received a state tax incentive worth eight million dollars only four years ago, in exchange for a promise to keep jobs in the region. The state's economic development agency said it is reviewing the agreement and may ask for some of the money back. The company is offering severance of one week of pay per year of service and job placement help. Local businesses near the plant, including a diner and a hardware store, said they expect to lose a large share of their customers. Some economists argue that the shift reflects global competition that no single town can reverse. A few former workers have enrolled in a nursing program at the community college.

topic: a celebrity chef accused of stealing recipes from a small family restaurant
wrong_topic: the physics of black holes
text: A well-known television chef is facing accusations that several dishes in her best-selling new cookbook were copied from a small family restaurant in another state. The owners of the restaurant, a married couple who opened it thirty years ago, posted side-by-side photos showing near-identical ingredient lists and plating for three dishes, including a braised lamb that has been on their menu since the beginning. They said the chef ate at their restaurant twice while filming a travel show and asked detailed questions about how the dishes were made. The chef's publisher said that recipes are generally not protected by copyright and that the dishes in question draw on traditional techniques used by many cooks in the region. In a short video, the chef said she had been inspired by many meals during her travels and regretted not crediting the restaurant by name. Some food writers said that borrowing is common and that no recipe is truly original. Others said that powerful figures in the industry routinely profit from the work of less visible cooks, especially immigrants. Since the controversy began, the family restaurant has been fully booked for weeks. The publisher has said a future printing of the cookbook may include an acknowledgment. The couple said they want an apology more than money.

topic: a government lowering the voting age to sixteen in local elections
wrong_topic: the best hiking trails in the mountains
text: The state legislature passed a bill on Wednesday that will allow sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds to vote in city and school board elections starting next year. The bill passed by a narrow margin after a long debate. Supporters said young people are directly affected by local decisions about schools, transit, and parks, and that people who start voting early are more likely to keep voting throughout their lives. They pointed to two cities that adopted a similar rule, where turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds was higher than among voters aged eighteen to twenty-four. Opponents argued that most teenagers still live with their parents and may simply vote the way their parents tell them to, and that the line between childhood and adulthood should not be moved for some purposes but not others. One lawmaker noted that sixteen-year-olds cannot sign contracts or serve on juries. A survey of high school students in the state found that roughly half supported the change, while a third said they did not feel ready to vote. Election officials said they will need new funding to update registration systems. The governor has not said whether he will sign the bill. A student who testified at the hearing said that young people are told to care about their communities but are not given a say in them.

topic: a zoo deciding to euthanize a healthy giraffe to prevent inbreeding
wrong_topic: a tutorial on spreadsheet formulas
text: A city zoo confirmed on Monday that it had euthanized an eighteen-month-old male giraffe, despite offers from two other institutions to take the animal. Zoo officials said the giraffe's genes were already well represented in the European breeding program and that allowing him to breed would increase the risk of inbreeding. They said the offers came from facilities that do not meet the program's standards, and that castration or contraception would have caused other welfare problems. After the giraffe was killed, his body was dissected in front of visitors, including children, as part of an educational session, and the meat was fed to the zoo's lions. Animal rights groups called the decision cruel and unnecessary, and an online petition calling for the director's resignation has gathered more than one hundred thousand signatures. Several zoo scientists defended the decision, saying that breeding programs must manage populations carefully and that it is more honest to show the public how such decisions work. Some visitors who watched the dissection said their children asked thoughtful questions about anatomy. Others said the display was shocking. The zoo director said he had received death threats and stood by the decision. Wildlife ethicists noted that zoos routinely make similar choices with less charismatic species, and that the public reaction says as much about which animals people care about as it does about the zoo.

topic: a company requiring employees to return to the office five days a week
wrong_topic: the geology of volcanic islands
text: A large software company told its employees on Tuesday that everyone will be required to work from the office five days a week starting in January, ending a hybrid policy that allowed three days at home. The chief executive wrote in a memo that in-person work leads to faster decisions and better mentoring for junior staff, and that the company's most important projects over the past year were developed by teams who met regularly in person. Within hours, an internal petition opposing the change had collected several thousand signatures. Employees who moved away from the city during the pandemic with their managers' approval said they now face a choice between relocating and resigning. Some parents said the change would make it impossible to manage school pickups. A company spokesperson said exceptions will be granted for medical reasons, but not for location. Researchers who study remote work said the evidence on productivity is mixed and depends heavily on the type of job. Some analysts suggested that the policy may be a quiet way to reduce headcount without announcing layoffs, a claim the company denied. A few employees said they welcomed the change because they felt isolated at home. The company's share price rose slightly after the announcement. Office space near the headquarters is in short supply, and some teams may have to share desks.

topic: a national park limiting the number of daily visitors with a lottery system
wrong_topic: the chemistry of baking soda
text: Beginning next summer, visitors who want to drive into the most popular area of a national park will need a permit drawn through an online lottery. The park service says that traffic jams on the main road regularly stretch for several miles and that rangers spend much of their time managing parking instead of protecting wildlife. Last year the park received more than four million visits, nearly double the number from a decade ago. Under the new system, about sixty percent of permits will be awarded months in advance, with the rest released two days before each date. Tourism businesses in nearby towns worry that the lottery will discourage spontaneous trips and that visitors who fail to win a permit will simply go elsewhere. Some longtime visitors said that the experience inside the park had become unpleasant because of crowds, and they welcomed the change. Others pointed out that the online system favors people with reliable internet and flexible schedules, and that families with less money may find it harder to plan trips months ahead. Tribes with historical ties to the land will be exempt from the permit requirement. The park service said it will review the program after two seasons. The first lottery opens in March.

topic: a city replacing car lanes on a main street with a protected bike lane
wrong_topic: the history of ancient Egyptian pyramids
text: Construction crews finished painting the last stretch of a new protected bike lane on Market Street this week, after the city removed one lane of car traffic in each direction. The project was approved last year after a cyclist was killed at an intersection near the train station. City engineers say the redesign will slow traffic and reduce crashes, and early counts show bicycle trips on the street have tripled since the first section opened. Several shop owners along the corridor say their sales have dropped because customers can no longer park in front of their stores, and that delivery trucks now block the remaining lane. A survey by the local business association found that most of its members opposed the change, but a separate study by a university transport group found that most shoppers on the street arrive on foot, by bus, or by bicycle. Drivers who commute through the area complain that travel times during rush hour have increased by several minutes. Supporters argue that the street was designed decades ago around cars and that safety should come before convenience. The fire department said it was consulted and that emergency vehicles can still pass. The mayor said the city will collect data for a full year before considering any changes. A petition to restore the car lanes has been submitted to the council.

topic: a public library removing a children's book after parent complaints
wrong_topic: how to repair a bicycle tire
text: The board of a county library system voted five to two on Thursday to move a picture book about a family with two fathers from the children's section to the adult section. The decision followed complaints from a group of parents who said the book introduced topics that should be discussed at home rather than in a library. The book, which won a national award for illustration, has been checked out more than two hundred times since it was added to the collection. Librarians who spoke at the meeting said the system has a written policy for reviewing challenged materials, and that a review committee had recommended keeping the book where it was. The board overrode that recommendation. Some parents at the meeting said they simply wanted to be able to choose what their young children see, and that the book was not being banned because adults could still borrow it. Others said that moving it sends a message to children from families like the one in the book that their families are not appropriate. A national library association issued a statement criticizing the decision. The author said she was saddened but not surprised. Two board members who voted for the move said they would support creating a parental review process for all new children's books. A local bookstore has placed the book in its front window.

topic: a professional sports league allowing betting company sponsorships on team jerseys
wrong_topic: the anatomy of the human heart
text: The national basketball league announced that, starting next season, teams may sell the advertising patch on their jerseys to sports betting companies. Until now, betting firms were limited to arena signs and television commercials. League officials said the change reflects new state laws that have legalized sports betting in much of the country, and that the sponsorships could bring in tens of millions of dollars for smaller-market teams. Public health researchers warned that young fans, including children who buy replica jerseys, would see betting brands every time they watch their favorite players. A coalition of addiction counselors said calls to gambling helplines have risen sharply since online betting became legal. The league said that all partners must follow responsible gambling rules and that a portion of the revenue will fund prevention programs. Some players expressed concern that the integrity of games could be questioned, especially after a recent scandal in a minor league where an official was found to have shared injury information with gamblers. Team owners largely welcomed the decision. A few teams said they would not sign betting sponsors out of respect for their local communities. Advertising analysts expect the first deals to be announced within weeks. One former player said that he grew up watching games with his father and could not imagine wearing a betting logo on his chest.

topic: a city paying people experiencing homelessness to move to other cities
wrong_topic: a guide to identifying wild mushrooms
text: For the past two years, a coastal city has offered free bus tickets to people experiencing homelessness who say they have family or friends willing to house them in another city. Officials describe the program as family reunification and say more than nine hundred people have used it. A newspaper investigation published this week found that the city rarely checked whether a relative was actually waiting at the other end. Reporters reached several people who had traveled through the program and found that some were back on the streets within weeks in cities where they had no support. Officials in two receiving cities said they were never told that people were being sent to them. The program's director said that for many participants a ticket home was exactly what they needed, and that the city follows up by phone whenever possible. Advocates for unhoused people argued that the program mainly moves a visible problem out of town without addressing housing costs or mental health care. Some business owners in the city's downtown said that the area had become noticeably cleaner and safer since the program began. A council member has requested an audit of the program and records of all follow-up calls. The mayor said she supports helping people reconnect with family and would welcome improvements. The program costs about two hundred thousand dollars a year.

topic: a hospital charging patients a fee for sending messages to their doctors
wrong_topic: the training schedule of a marathon runner
text: A regional health system has started billing patients for some of the messages they send to their doctors through its online portal. Under the new policy, a message that requires more than a few minutes of a physician's medical judgment, such as a question about a new symptom or a medication change, may be billed as a short virtual visit. Simple requests such as scheduling or prescription refills remain free. The health system said the volume of portal messages has nearly tripled since the pandemic and that doctors now spend hours each evening answering them without being paid for the work. Several physicians said that the burden contributes to burnout and that some colleagues have reduced their clinical hours because of it. Patients, however, were caught off guard. Some said they received charges of thirty to fifty dollars after asking what they thought were brief questions. Patient advocates argued that the policy may discourage people, especially those with low incomes, from asking questions that could prevent more serious problems. The health system said that patients are warned before a message is billed and can choose to schedule a visit instead, though several patients said they never saw a warning. Insurance coverage for the charges varies by plan. Other health systems in the region are watching closely and some have adopted similar policies.

topic: a high school ending its honors classes to place all students in mixed classes
wrong_topic: the migration of salmon upstream
text: Beginning in the fall, a suburban high school will eliminate separate honors sections for ninth and tenth grade English and science. All students in those grades will be placed in the same classes, and those who want extra challenge can complete optional honors assignments within the regular course. District leaders said that the honors track had become sharply divided by race and family income, with some students placed on a lower track as early as middle school and rarely moving up. They cited studies suggesting that mixed classes can raise achievement for lower-performing students without harming higher performers. Many parents of students in honors classes objected at a crowded board meeting, saying their children would be bored and held back, and some said they were considering private schools. Several teachers said they support the goal but worry about teaching a wider range of skill levels in classes of thirty students without more aides. A senior who had moved from the regular track to honors said that the switch changed how teachers saw her and how she saw herself. Other students said that honors classes were one of the few places they felt challenged. The district promised additional training for teachers and a review of test scores after two years. Advanced Placement courses in the last two years of high school will remain unchanged.

topic: a music festival canceled after heavy rain, with organizers refusing refunds
wrong_topic: how to brew green tea properly
text: Organizers of a three-day music festival canceled the event on its second morning after overnight storms turned the campground and parking fields into mud. Thousands of attendees, many of whom had traveled hundreds of miles, were told to leave the site by noon. In a statement, the organizers said the cancellation was necessary for safety after an emergency vehicle became stuck and could not reach a stage area. They also said that tickets were non-refundable under the terms of sale, which list weather as a circumstance beyond their control, and that they would offer a discount on next year's event instead. Many attendees said that the forecast had predicted heavy rain for days and that organizers should have prepared the site with more gravel and drainage or canceled earlier, before people arrived. Some musicians who did not get to perform said they had still been paid. A consumer protection lawyer said that terms of sale do not always override state consumer laws and that ticket buyers may have a case. Credit card companies are reviewing a large number of disputed charges. Local hotels and restaurants, which had expected a busy weekend, also lost business. The festival's founder posted a video apologizing for how the cancellation was communicated, but he did not change the refund policy. A group of attendees has hired a lawyer.

text: A new law passed by the national parliament will require anyone who opens a social media account to verify their identity with a government-issued document. The platforms will store a confirmation of identity, not the document itself, and users will still be allowed to post under a pseudonym. Supporters of the law said it will make it easier to hold people accountable for harassment, fraud, and threats, which they said have become common online. Victims of online abuse who testified before the committee described receiving hundreds of messages from accounts that were deleted and recreated as soon as they were reported. Opponents warned that the law would create large databases that could be hacked or misused by future governments, and that it may discourage whistleblowers and activists from speaking freely. Some pointed out that many people, including older adults and recent immigrants, lack valid identity documents. The largest platforms said they will comply but questioned whether verification will reduce abuse, since much of it comes from accounts linked to real names. A technology researcher said that similar rules in another country had a modest effect on abusive posts but also reduced participation among younger users. The law takes effect in eighteen months. Digital rights groups have announced a court challenge on privacy grounds.

text: A major museum announced on Tuesday that it will return a collection of bronze sculptures to the country from which they were removed during a military expedition more than a century ago. The sculptures have been among the museum's most visited objects for decades, and a dedicated gallery was built for them in the nineteen-seventies. The museum's director said that new research into the collection's history confirmed that the pieces were taken by force, and that keeping them was no longer consistent with the institution's values. Officials from the receiving country welcomed the decision and said the sculptures will be displayed in a new national museum currently under construction. Some scholars said the return was long overdue and that it should lead to similar decisions about other objects in the collection. Others warned that the new museum has not yet opened and questioned whether the sculptures will be adequately protected. A few trustees reportedly argued that the museum's large international audience allows more people to see the works than would otherwise be possible. Legal experts noted that the museum is not required by law to return the objects and acted voluntarily. The transfer is expected to take place next year. In the meantime, the museum plans to display the sculptures alongside new labels describing how they were acquired.
